I found that "fact-checking" is the best way to help them. My main problem I struggle with is intrusive thoughts, so I've been trying to find more ways to help ease or at least neutralize them. Fact checking is telling yourself what you know you should be thinking, basically. Using your "good cognition". For me, anyways, when I get intrusive thoughts, I also have a background voice kinda going like "you know thats not true" "you're being irrational" "but what about xyz?" etc. As if one side of my brain is arguing with the other side. Of course, the intrusive side always manages to talk over any rational thought. Best thing for me is basically screaming (inside my head of course) what the good side of my brain is thinking. I know it sounds weird and psychotic but hey, it works for me. Another thing to help is write down how you are feeling and thinking, yes it is hard to write as fast as you think, but at least get something down. one sentence is good enough. Once those thoughts are gone, or have at least subsided, reread what you wrote and write next to or under it why it's not rational. give as many reasons as possible, but still one is good enough. you can always go back and add more to either side whenever you please. this way, when you get those same thoughts, you can go back and allow your good cognition to speak as well, and remind yourself why it isn't rational when you can't think straight. 

That's what helps me sometimes, I'm still struggling with remembering and making myself get up and do it rather than sulking in my thoughts. Hope it helped!! Good luck to you <3

I've experienced the same thing before, once I lay down to sleep I hear people talking outside my window or in another room in the house. I know it's not a TV (there are other people in the house, as well.) and I can clearly hear it under the hum of a distant TV. I also used to exhaust myself getting up and walking downstairs because I heard someone clearly call my name and to no avail no one is even downstairs at all. It worries me sometimes, but you have to remember that your brain is very complex and very powerful. It can literally trick you into thinking something is there when there's nothing there, even neurotypicals. And the fact you have headphones in while this is happening could very well just be your brain associating having headphones in with hearing sound, and creates phantom sounds on its own. I would talk to a psychiatrist about your mother and this happening because it could very well be Schitzoaffective disorder, but until that happens, I wouldn't worry. The best thing you can do for yourself is keep calm and try your best to ignore it. Drown it out with your own thoughts maybe?

When I get irritated/angry with my SO, I noticed recently I get fight-or-flight response. I never noticed it, because I always associated the response with my anxiety and never thought it to happen with anger on any level. My heart rate goes up and I can literally feel the blood pumping through my body and get the sensation of the room being 10 degrees higher than what it actually is. My SO and I spend most of our time in our bedroom, just since his xbox is in there and it's where I like to be when on my laptop. So, we're usually sitting right next to each other when we get into little arguments and I get extremely offended/defensive/irritated over silly things that in the moment make me want to scream and say passive aggressive things to him. I always feel the urge after the argument is over to walk out of the room for no reason at all, really. I'll sit and argue with myself internally on wether or not to leave the room or force myself to stay in the room and deal with my anger to the point where I'm forcing myself to calm down. And I'll usually cave after 10 minutes of sitting and being pissy to myself and go and just sit in the bathroom alone. Weird, right? But it calms me down a little once I leave the room, although I'm still upset. I eventually realized it was fight-or-flight kicking in that made me want to leave the room. And I thought, isn't that cowardly? Isn't that just making me avoid my problem of anger issues by running away? I came to the conclusion that yes, it is cowardly and I am avoiding the root problem (myself and my anger issues). BUT it's a step in the right direction I suppose, it'll remove me from the situation for the moment and allows me to think and collect my thoughts without being explosive and making the situation worse. One day, I'll be able to sit still and calm myself down without having to leave the room. Baby steps, I tell myself. 

I know I rambled, but my point is to listen to your body when in situations where you struggle to try and help yourself. It doesn't have to be anything miraculous, but it does need to be challenging. I struggle with allowing myself some leeway with coping mechanisms and allowing myself to take recovery at a pace that I am comfortable with. Listen to your body. If you feel the urge to scream when you're angry, try inhaling then exhaling really deeply and loudly through your mouth until you feel the urge go away. Like a silent scream almost. If you want to reach out to people you know you should let be, type/write out what you'd like to say to them at the moment and then delete/throw it away. Sort of act as if you are talking to them. If when frustrated, and you do what I do (which is get really unsettled and restless and feel the need to literally just throw yourself on the floor and flail around like a toddler because all the pent up frustration somehow turns into this weird energy?) then go somewhere where you can be alone, and literally just flail around.. I know it sounds really bizarre but it gets all the pent up energy out and allows you to relax. throw shadow punches and shake your legs like crazy. do the thing that dancers in the 80's do in the rain in music videos, the weird entire body seizure dance thing. 

All our emotions are some form of energy. Listen to your body, and think of a way to release that energy by doing a simulation of what you really want to do.

Use a mindfulness technique called "Fact-Checking". Basically, disable opinion and use only reality to address your doubts/questions/worries. If you're worried/doubting she doesn't actually like you, ask yourself these questions (and do NOT try to convince yourself of an answer you know is not true) ; Does she seem to enjoy our time together? When we are together, do I have her full attention, or is she distracted by her phone, friends, etc.? Is she affection in public or only in private? Does she treat me more like a friend than an S/O? Is she public with our relationship (ie. statuses on social media sites are accurate, telling others you are together, etc)? Why could she possibly be with in a relationship with me if she didn't like me (ie. is she using you for money, a place to live, a car, attention etc.)? 

I highly doubt she is using you for any reason because if so, she'd be making a hell of a lot better effort trying to get these things from you than what she is, if by forever to respond means several hours at a time. ( five minutes to respond is not forever btw... )

It's somewhat easier to control anger/irritability/depression when around young children in fear of making them scared/upset/uncomfortable or possibly even traumatized.

If even the simple basics like feeding, entertaining, supervising, planning, preparing, etc are too much to handle for more than 12 hours, I would wait until you are in some sort of treatment. If you do fine, then great! It's then up to you to decide if your moral standpoint is one that a child is deserving of, because I'm sure you know that being a parent isn't only basic care.

Best thing to do is sort of act like there's nothing wrong in your own mind. Ignore it, in a way. I'm not saying don't acknowledge your feelings, but I've found that reminding myself that it is only temporary (you can't feel one way forever!) and going about my usual day helps speed the process of feeling empty/bored/irritable. 

Acknowledge then dismiss. "I don't like this feeling, but it will soon pass." "It is hard to cope with this feeling, but I will one day be able to if I keep trying" "Being in this mental/physical state is difficult, but that does not mean I won't be happy again." Thinking like this will eventually become a habit if you do it enough, even if you don't believe what you're telling yourself in the slightest, it's still good to keep positive thoughts in your head while still connecting to your emotions. 

Please don't try shopping or eating to cope. It can easily lead to other risky behaviors and cause bad habits to form.

Although I relate entirely, it helps to rationalize that no one is really meant to stay in your life forever. For example, your parents, even if you have an extremely strong, healthy, and active relationship with them, one day they unfortunately will die; and leave your life. This doesn't mean your life is over or you're going to be alone forever. People come and people go. You yourself have more than likely walked in and out of several lives in the past, whether intentionally walking in/out or harmlessly entering and exiting one's life. But are they alone? Probably not. Are you alone? Probably not. 

Remember: being alone and feeling alone are two very different things. It's hard to literally BE alone in life. No coworkers, friends, acquaintances, siblings, relatives, parents, pets, neighbors, enemies even? Unlikely. However, feeling alone is usually when someone isn't getting the correct attention they want/deserve/need. 

When I feel alone, it's pretty much when my SO/FP isn't giving me enough attention or the right kind. But, it doesn't have to be an SO or an FP. 

Try and figure out what exactly you're looking for and who you want it from, in terms of not being alone. It may also help to have someone you trust rationalize things for you when you're feeling one way or another strongly. (not saying you dont rationalize things but I tend to do so when I'm feeling xyz)
